Reading the evidence
The ground made signals.
We made a catalog.
A seismometer records ground motion. A catalog is a set of estimates extracted from those recordings. For this sequence, David Shelly searched stored signals using the waveforms of known earthquakes, then refined the events’ relative locations. His interpretation: the alignments illuminate a complex system of crossing faults. The dots alone do not tell us exactly where every fault surface lies.


An input13,525
Routinely cataloged earthquakes supplied waveform templates.
→
A searchSimilar?
Match templates against historical recordings; use relative timing to sharpen locations.
→
A result34,091
Detected and located events in the release you can explore here.


The template count is an input to the study. This file does not identify which individual points were templates or additional detections. Nor does it estimate how many events escaped detection. Raising the magnitude slider cannot recreate the original routine catalog.
This is a reconstruction made after the sequence. Calling an earlier earthquake a foreshock uses knowledge of what came later. The pictures explain observations; they are not an earthquake prediction or hazard forecast.
The little earthquakes help us see.
The missing information tells us how carefully to look.


Sources, exact data, and the limits of this notebook
What you are exploring
David R. Shelly (2020), A High-Resolution Seismic Catalog for the Initial 2019 Ridgecrest Earthquake Sequence, USGS data release. File DataS1_noXYZ.txt, version dated September 4, 2019 in its header; retrieved September 29, 2026 UTC. Every one of its 34,091 records is embedded here. First origin: July 4, 15:35:29.400 UTC. Last: July 16, 23:59:26.500 UTC. These are the initial sequence, not all Ridgecrest earthquakes.
The official data page marks the release CC0 1.0. The XML metadata imposes no use constraints. Original observations were retrieved from SCEDC: Southern California Earthquake Data Center (2013), doi:10.7909/C3WD3xH. All visual design and drawing here are original.
Locations are estimates
The file calls them earthquake “hypocentroids.” Its header says the events were not individually checked and large errors may exist. No numerical location uncertainty or quality flag is supplied. We preserve every reported value, including the 227 depths greater than 25 km and the maximum of 556.580 km. These are reasons for scrutiny, not evidence of a deep Ridgecrest fault.
The 0–25 km section is a display window. Deeper records remain in the map, time plot and inspector, with the number outside the section stated. “Show full depth” switches the section to 0–600 km. The displayed vertical scale factor changes accordingly. No depth is clamped to a surface or silently corrected.
A depth-reference discrepancy
The record-file header specifies a nominal surface 0.7 km above sea level; the USGS Ridgecrest figure description agrees. The accompanying XML instead mentions Kilauea and 1.2 km. We follow the Ridgecrest-specific header and figure. This is a horizontal reference plane, not a terrain model; depths are not converted to current ComCat origins.
What the filters mean
Counts above the map first apply time and magnitude, then the section band. “Fit selection” magnifies the horizontal map, section and time extents around the band selection without removing records. The section adds its stated depth window. The time plot shows the band selection at all depths. Gray points are only context; ringed points retain the chosen record even if it falls outside the filters. “Before” excludes the M6.4; “between” includes M6.4 and excludes M7.1; “onward” includes M7.1. Counts: 35, 4,692 and 29,364 respectively.
All rows have time, location, depth, magnitude and release ID. IDs are not CISN IDs. The magnitudes mix retained SCSN preferred estimates with calibrated detections; the per-event magnitude type is absent. The header states a factor of 10 in amplitude corresponds to 0.831 magnitude units for its detection calibration. This notebook applies no energy conversion. Dot sizes are constant; selection rings and named-event labels are annotations.
Derived coordinates, unchanged records
A local equirectangular projection uses reference 35.75° N, 117.60° W and Earth radius 6,371.0088 km. East distance = R cos(35.75°) × longitude offset in radians; north distance = R × latitude offset in radians. This approximation is for viewing this small region, not a relocation. The section projects those distances onto an axis at the selected bearing clockwise from north; its band uses the perpendicular distance. Map scales match in both directions. Section vertical exaggeration/compression is stated.
Times are UTC; elapsed time is relative to this file’s M7.1 at 2019-07-06 03:19:52.860 UTC (July 5, 20:19:52.860 PDT). The M6.4 precedes it by 33.768 hours. All original time, coordinate, depth and magnitude precision is preserved in the embedded integers. More decimal places do not imply equivalent accuracy.
Related interpretation
Shelly (2020), Foreshocks, aftershocks, and faulting complexity, Seismological Research Letters 91, 1971–1978, doi:10.1785/0220190309. The USGS geonarrative covers the wider field response. This notebook adds linked record inspection and section/filter experiments.
